title: Letrus automated essay scoring and feedback in 110 Espírito Santo public high schools raises ENEM essay scores by 0.094 standard deviations in a 2019 randomized trial
summary: In a 2019 trial in 178 public high schools in Espírito Santo, Brazil, Letrus automated essay scoring and feedback raised ENEM essay scores by 0.094 standard deviations.
account: Bruno Ferman, Lycia Lima and Flavio Riva of the São Paulo schools of economics and business administration at FGV ran a randomized trial from March to November 2019 with the Espírito Santo state education department and an education technology company. Exame reports that the company was Letrus and that J-PAL funded the trial. The trial covered 178 public high schools with about 19,000 senior students. In 55 schools, students wrote practice essays for the national college entrance exam (ENEM) on a platform whose automated writing evaluation system gave instant feedback and a predicted score. Another 55 schools received the same system plus grades and comments from human graders, and 68 schools served as the comparison group. Both versions raised essay scores by 0.094 standard deviations, pooled across the official 2019 ENEM essay and an independently administered essay of the same format. The human graders added no further gain. The authors report that teachers shifted time from routine grading toward individual discussions with students about their essays. The paper is a working paper that the authors posted in February 2021, and it does not name the company.
purpose: The system was built to grade practice essays for the ENEM and give students feedback, so that teachers could spend less time on routine grading. Higher essay scores were that purpose.
system: Letrus automated writing evaluation (AWE) platform, with machine-learning essay scoring and automated feedback (tested alone and with human graders)
deployer: Espírito Santo State Education Department (SEDU/ES) with Letrus, in 110 public high schools

ratings.reason: Senior students in schools with either version of the system scored 0.094 standard deviations higher on the ENEM essay than students in comparison schools.
The authors report that teachers moved time from routine grading toward individual discussions with students about essay quality.

ai_role.statement: Schools were randomly assigned to the automated system alone, to the system with human graders, or to no system. The fully automated arm produced the same gain as the arm with human graders, which isolates the contribution of the automated scoring and feedback within the program. The gain also runs through changes in what teachers did with the time saved.
